tip: Aangenaam kennis te maken is a set greeting; the verb kennismaken splits around te into kennis te maken.
Ga zitten literally means go sit, and it is the everyday way to say take a seat.
For where you are from, use komen uit: ik kom uit Nederland. Uit marks origin.
A modal like 'mag' pairs with a main verb that goes to the very end: mag ik binnenkomen (may I come in).

english: I do not want to bother anyone.
tip: niemand (nobody) is already negative, so you add no niet: ik wil niemand lastigvallen.
Ik ben er weer means I am back; here weer means again.
Age uses zijn plus jaar oud, and jaar stays singular after a number: dertig jaar, not jaren.
Dutch builds time words with van: vanavond (tonight), vandaag, vanmorgen, each written as one word.
Language names are capitalized and take no article: ik leer Nederlands op school.

english: See you soon, we'll be in touch!
tip: tot plus a time makes a farewell: tot gauw (see you soon), tot morgen, tot straks.
eten is both the verb to eat and the noun the meal: het eten is klaar.
elke (every) always takes a singular noun: elke morgen, never a plural.
In the Netherlands lopen means to walk; use rennen for to run.
Praten pairs with over for the topic: praten over het weer = to talk about the weather.
Hunger uses hebben, not zijn: ik heb honger is literally I have hunger.
kleding (clothing) is uncountable: no plural, always singular, like English clothing.

english: Good afternoon, can I help you?
tip: Yes or no questions put the verb first: Kan ik u helpen? The subject follows the verb.

english: Nice to speak to you again.
tip: After leuk, use te plus an infinitive: leuk je te spreken (nice to speak with you).

english: Bye, I have to go now.
tip: dag works as both hello and goodbye; here Dag, ik moet nu gaan is a casual bye.

english: Hello, I am looking for the station.
tip: zoeken already means to look for, so no extra preposition: ik zoek het station.

english: Hello, I'm coming to pick you up.
tip: 'je' is the informal you for friends and family, as in ik kom je ophalen. Switch to 'u' with strangers or elders.

english: We are going out to eat tonight.
tip: uit eten gaan is a fixed phrase for going out for a meal: wij gaan vanavond uit eten.

english: He is going to visit his parents.
tip: zijn means both to be and his; here zijn ouders is his parents.

target: Prettig kennis met u te maken.
tip: 'u' is the polite you for strangers and formal settings: kennis met u te maken (pleased to meet you).

target: De zon schijnt vandaag heel mooi.
tip: Dutch adjectives double as adverbs with no ending: mooi is both beautiful and beautifully.

target: Doei, ik zie je morgen weer!
english: Bye, I'll see you again tomorrow!
tip: Modern Dutch leans toward 'je' even with strangers, as in ik zie je weer, but default to 'u' in service, writing, or with elders.

target: Ik wens je een fijne dag.
english: I wish you a nice day.
tip: Adjectives add -e before a de-word: een fijne dag (de dag).

target: Ik bel mijn moeder elke zondag.
english: I call my mother every Sunday.
tip: Weekdays are lowercase in Dutch: zondag, maandag, unlike English.

target: Ik geloof dat hij gelijk heeft.
english: I believe that he is right.
tip: 'dat' (that) sends the verb to the clause end: dat hij gelijk heeft, with 'heeft' landing last.

target: Ik controleer mijn email elke ochtend.
english: I check my email every morning.
tip: controleren means to check, not to control: ik controleer mijn email.
